sections.b: Tacitus says Vespasian sent Titus from Judea to Galba; at Corinth Titus learned that Galba was dead and weighed his choices (2:1). Some said he turned back for love of Queen Berenice (2:2). He sailed by Rhodes and Cyprus and went to the temple of Venus at Paphos, where the priest Sostratus told him privately that great things lay ahead (2:2-4). He then rejoined his father as a pledge of success. Suetonius also has Titus consult the oracle of Paphian Venus about his voyage (Titus 5). Titus helped end the quarrel between Mucianus and his father (2:5) and was left to press on in Judea (2:82). Not the Bible's Titus: Paul's Titus went to Dalmatia (2 Timothy 4:10).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:1-5; Histories of Tacitus 2:82; 2 Timothy 4:10

sections.h: Vespasian in Book 2: the soldier, the omens, the oath
sections.b: Tacitus draws Vespasian as a sharp, plain soldier who marched at the head of the column, ate what came to hand and looked like a common soldier; "but for his greed, he was the equal of the generals of old" (2:5). At sixty with two young sons, he weighed the risk of a bid for the throne (2:74-75). Mucianus urged him on (2:76-77); omens came back to mind: a cypress that fell and rose again, and the priest Basilides at Carmel (2:78). The legions at Alexandria swore to him on July 1st and the army of Judea on July 3rd (2:79), and his soldiers hailed him as he came out of his room (2:80). Suetonius tells the same cypress, the Carmel oracle and Tiberius Alexander's oath (Vespasian 5-6). Josephus has the troops proclaim him with threats, and says Vespasian freed him as a man who had foretold the throne (Jewish War 4.10).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:5; Histories of Tacitus 2:74-82; Matthew 24:6

sections.h: Book 2: from Bedriacum to Vespasian's oath
sections.b: Book 2 runs from Titus on the road in January AD 69 to Caecina's treachery in the autumn. Otho's armies took the field (2:11-12); Caecina failed at Placentia (2:17-22) and lost at the Castors (2:24-26); the Vitellianists won at Bedriacum (2:41-45) and Otho killed himself (2:46-50). The Wikipedia article on the year puts the battle on 14 April; it puts Otho's death the next day in its introduction and on 16 April in its timeline, so this page says mid-April. Vitellius marched to Rome with 60,000 men (2:87-89), while the East moved to Vespasian: Alexandria swore on July 1st (2:79) and Syria before July 15th (2:81). Plutarch's Otho and Suetonius's lives of Otho and Vitellius tell the same events.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:11-50; Histories of Tacitus 2:79-81; Histories of Tacitus 2:87-89

sections.b: In his Olivet Discourse Jesus tells his disciples "You are going to hear of wars and reports of wars" (Matthew 24:6). Book 2 shows the East watching those wars come from the West (2:6). It also names places and people the New Testament names: Corinth (2:1), Paphos (2:2), Caesarea and Antioch (2:79), King Agrippa and Queen Berenice (2:81), and the provinces of Galatia, Pamphylia, Pontus and Cappadocia (2:6, 2:9).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:6; Histories of Tacitus 2:81; Matthew 24:6; Acts 25:13

sections.b: Tacitus shows Otho marching on foot in an iron breastplate (2:11), sending his army against Caecina, losing at Bedriacum while he stayed at Brixellum (2:33, 2:41-44), and then refusing his soldiers' offer to fight on: he said he would not risk the young men's lives again (2:47). He gave out money and letters, comforted his nephew, drank cold water, slept, and killed himself at dawn with a dagger (2:48-49). Plutarch and Suetonius agree on the dagger, the dawn and the soldiers who died with him (Plutarch, Otho 17; Suetonius, Otho 11-12). Tacitus gives his age as the 37th year (2:49); Plutarch says 37 and Suetonius 38.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:33; Histories of Tacitus 2:46-50; 1 Samuel 31:4

sections.b: Tacitus says Vitellius punished Otho's boldest centurions but spared the property of the beaten (2:60, 2:62), expelled the astrologers and banned Knights from the arena (2:62), visited the battlefield at Bedriacum without a shudder (2:70) and made offerings to Nero (2:95). He entered Rome with an army of 60,000 and many camp followers (2:87-89). His banquets were costly (2:62, 2:95), and he is said to have spent 900 million sesterces in a few months (2:95). Suetonius agrees on the battlefield, the rites for Nero and the astrologers (Vitellius 10, 11, 14). Tacitus says too that he held the consular elections as an ordinary citizen (2:91). Keep in view that Tacitus writes against Vitellius.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:60-71; Histories of Tacitus 2:87-95

sections.b: Five Praetorian cohorts and picked men of the guard marched with Otho (2:11), took part in the fights at Placentia and Bedriacum (2:22, 2:24, 2:44), and their prefect Plotius Firmus begged Otho not to abandon them (2:46). Vitellius disarmed his predecessor's cohorts (2:67); they returned as the backbone of the Flavian cause. He then built a new guard of sixteen Praetorian and four city cohorts, each of a thousand men (2:93), taken from the whole army (2:94). Paul's chains were known "by the whole praetorium" (Philippians 1:13), a word that may mean this guard or the governor's quarters.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:11; Histories of Tacitus 2:46; Histories of Tacitus 2:67; Histories of Tacitus 2:93-94; Philippians 1:13

sections.b: Tacitus counts three legions in Judea, four in Syria and two in Egypt (2:4, 2:6, 2:76). Otho brought four legions from Dalmatia and Pannonia (2:11); Vitellius's army was of Rhine legions and Batavian cohorts (2:17, 2:27, 2:100). The tribune, centurion, cohort and legion appear in the Gospels and Acts too, as in Matthew 8:5-9, Acts 10:1 and Acts 21:31-32. The legions' own names, such as the Rapax and the Adjutrix (2:43), show the unit's pride.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:4; Histories of Tacitus 2:6; Histories of Tacitus 2:11; Histories of Tacitus 2:43; Matthew 8:9; Acts 10:1; Acts 21:31-32

sections.b: Book 2 has a full set: the entrails of young goats read at Paphos (2:3-4); a strange bird at Regium Lepidum (2:50); the astrologers expelled from Italy by Vitellius (2:62); the cypress that fell and rose again, Basilides's reading of the entrails at Carmel and Vespasian's astrologer Seleucus (2:78); a day marked as unlucky (2:91). Suetonius tells the cypress and the Carmel oracle (Vespasian 5), and the expulsion of astrologers (Vitellius 14). The Bible forbids divination in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), and shows a king of Babylon who "examines the liver" (Ezekiel 21:21).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:3-4; Histories of Tacitus 2:62; Histories of Tacitus 2:78; Histories of Tacitus 2:91; Deuteronomy 18:10-12; Ezekiel 21:21

sections.b: Judea is the base of Vespasian's army (2:4-5). Tacitus says only Jerusalem was left in the Jewish war, hard to take "because of the mountain stronghold and the Jews' stubborn religion" (2:4). He calls Caesarea the capital of Judea (2:79), and the mountain Carmel lies "between Judea and Syria" (2:78). The army of Judea swore to Vespasian on July 3rd (2:79), and Agrippa and Berenice joined (2:81). For the Bible's Caesarea see Acts 10:1 and Acts 25:13; for Carmel see 1 Kings 18:19-40.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:4; Histories of Tacitus 2:78-79; Histories of Tacitus 2:81; Acts 10:1; Acts 25:13; 1 Kings 18:19-40

sections.b: Josephus tells the same months. He agrees with Tacitus that the soldiers of Judea proclaimed Vespasian and that Mucianus and Tiberius Alexander backed him, but differs in details: Josephus has Vespasian refuse at first and accept under threat, and has him write to Tiberius Alexander after the proclamation, while Tacitus and Suetonius put the oath at Alexandria on July 1st before Judea's (Jewish War 4.10, 4.616; Tacitus 2:79-80). Josephus says Vespasian freed him, remembering his prophecy of the throne (Jewish War 4.10), and Suetonius tells the prophecy too (Vespasian 5.6). Tacitus complains of writers who flattered the Flavians (2:101).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:79-80; Histories of Tacitus 2:101

sections.b: A Roman Knight, Annius Faustus, had informed under Nero and was brought before the Senate (2:10); Quintius Certus, a Knight, died with the captain Claudius Pyrrhicus on Corsica (2:16). Vitellius gave his freedman Asiaticus the gold rings of a Knight (2:57) and banned Knights from the gladiator school and the arena (2:62). James speaks of "a man with gold on his fingers" (James 2:2).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:10; Histories of Tacitus 2:57; Histories of Tacitus 2:62; James 2:2

sections.h: Procurators, prefects and governors in Book 2
sections.b: Book 2 names Marius Maturus as procurator of the Maritime Alps (2:12), Decumus Pacarius as procurator of Corsica (2:16), Lucceius Albinus as procurator of both Mauretanias (2:58-59), and Tiberius Alexander as prefect of Egypt (2:74, 2:79). Vespasian and Mucianus are generals commanding provinces (2:5). The New Testament names Pilate (Luke 3:1), Felix and Festus (Acts 24-25) and Sergius Paulus the proconsul (Acts 13:7).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:12; Histories of Tacitus 2:58-59; Histories of Tacitus 2:74; Luke 3:1; Acts 13:7; Acts 25:1

sections.b: Under Galba the senators had voted to look into the cases of informers, and Vibius Crispus now used the decree against Annius Faustus (2:10). Part of the Senate left Rome with Otho and was stranded at Mutina after his defeat; the council of Mutina called them Conscript Fathers, "an ill-timed compliment" (2:52-54). When Otho died the Senate voted Vitellius every honor (2:55). Vitellius attended debates and tolerated Helvidius Priscus's opposition (2:91).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:10; Histories of Tacitus 2:52-55; Histories of Tacitus 2:91

sections.b: Book 2 shows Tacitus stepping back from his story. At 2:37-38 he doubts that the armies would have chosen peace and traces civil war to an old craving for power. At 2:50 he will not collect marvels but will not reject what common report says. At 2:101 he says the writers who recorded this war under the Flavians twisted the causes into flattery, and offers his own reading of why Caecina and Bassus turned. He names no author of those records. He also gives a sketch of Vespasian and Mucianus (2:5).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:5; Histories of Tacitus 2:37-38; Histories of Tacitus 2:50; Histories of Tacitus 2:101

sections.h: A false Nero and rites for Nero (Book 2)
sections.b: Tacitus says that around this time Achaia and Asia were thrown into a false panic by a report that Nero was on his way (2:8). A slave from Pontus or a freedman from Italy, who sang and looked like Nero, gathered deserters, landed at Cythnus, where Calpurnius Asprenas took his ship and he was killed; his body, with striking eyes, hair and fierce face, was taken to Asia and Rome (2:8-9). Later Vitellius held funeral rites for Nero on the Campus Martius (2:95). Suetonius agrees that Vitellius made offerings to Nero (Vitellius 11). Revelation's beast that was wounded and healed (Revelation 13:3) and the eighth king (Revelation 17:11) are read in connection with this legend by some; see the Revelation sections of this page.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:8-9; Histories of Tacitus 2:71; Histories of Tacitus 2:95; Revelation 13:3; Revelation 17:11

sections.b: Tacitus says: "Between Judea and Syria is Carmel. That's the name of both the mountain and the god. Their ancestors handed it down that the god has no statue or temple, only an altar and reverence." There Vespasian sacrificed and the priest Basilides read the entrails and told him he would have a great dwelling, huge boundaries and many men. Suetonius says Vespasian consulted the oracle of the god of Carmel and got lots promising success (Vespasian 5.6). The Wikipedia article on Mount Carmel reports a Greek inscription to Heliopolitan Zeus of Carmel, published by Avi-Yonah. Elijah, on this mountain, "mended the LORD's altar, which had been knocked down" (1 Kings 18:30); whether the altar in Tacitus is a memory of it is only a guess.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:78; 1 Kings 18:19-40; 1 Kings 18:30

sections.h: Agrippa II and Berenice in Tacitus
sections.b: Tacitus names a King Agrippa and a Queen Berenice in two places. Berenice is said to have drawn Titus back from the road to Rome (2:2). In AD 69 Agrippa, "called away from Rome by secret messages from his people while Vitellius still knew nothing," crossed the sea to join Vespasian, and Berenice "backed the cause with no less spirit" (2:81). They are the Agrippa and Bernice of Acts 25-26 (very likely); Berenice's sister Drusilla is the wife of Felix (Acts 24:24), and their father is the Herod Agrippa of Acts 12.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:2; Histories of Tacitus 2:81; Acts 12:1-23; Acts 24:24; Acts 25:13-26:32

sections.b: Otho refused his soldiers' offer to fight on, spoke kindly to his friends, drank cold water, tested two daggers, slept, and "at first light he fell on the blade with his chest" (2:49). Tacitus calls it the more noble of his two bold acts (2:50), and some soldiers killed themselves beside the pyre (2:49). Saul "fell on" his sword (1 Samuel 31:4). None of the Bible accounts states a verdict on the act itself; see the page on suicide for how Jews and Christians have counseled since.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:46-50; 1 Samuel 31:4-5; Judges 9:54; 2 Samuel 17:23

sections.b: Tacitus calls Antioch the capital of Syria (2:79). Mucianus swore the eager soldiers to Vespasian there and spoke in the theater, where the people held their discussions (2:80); gold and silver were coined there for the war (2:82). Acts tells that "Antioch was the first place where the disciples came to be called 'Christians'" (Acts 11:26).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:79-82; Acts 11:26; Acts 13:1

sections.b: Tacitus shows the diviners at work: the priest of Paphos reads young goats' entrails (2:3-4); Vitellius expels the astrologers from Italy (2:62); Vespasian later keeps an astrologer, Seleucus (2:78). Deuteronomy 18:10-12 bans such practices in Israel, and Acts records the magician Bar-Jesus at Paphos (Acts 13:6-8).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:3-4; Histories of Tacitus 2:62; Histories of Tacitus 2:78; Deuteronomy 18:10-12; Acts 13:6-8

sections.b: Mucianus calls Augustus "the divine Augustus" (2:76); Vitellius put off the name Augustus and refused the name Caesar (2:62), and when the crowd pushed him to take Augustus (2:90), Tacitus calls both the refusal and the pushing empty gestures; the Augustales, a priesthood of the Julian family set up under Tiberius, light the fire at the rites for Nero (2:95). A man in Gaul, Mariccus, calls himself a god and is put to death (2:61). Acts reports a crowd's cry "It's a god speaking, not a man!" for Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:22).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:61; Histories of Tacitus 2:76; Histories of Tacitus 2:95; Acts 12:22

sections.b: Tacitus says that when Vitellius visited the battlefield, not forty days after the fight, he looked on many thousands of unburied citizens without shuddering and sacrificed to the gods of the place. The Bible treats lack of burial as disgrace: "there was nobody to bury them" (Psalm 79:3). At 2:45 a few were buried by their families and the legate Orfidius was cremated with the usual honors.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:45; Histories of Tacitus 2:70; Psalm 79:2-3; Jeremiah 16:4

sections.b: Mariccus, a commoner of the Boii, called himself the champion of Gaul and a god, gathered 8,000 men, and was crushed by the Aedui and cohorts sent by Vitellius. Thrown to wild beasts, he was not torn, and a crowd thought him unhurtable until he was killed before Vitellius. The Gospels warn that "false messiahs and false prophets will rise up" (Mark 13:22).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:61; Mark 13:21-22; Acts 5:36-37; Acts 8:9-10

sections.b: Jesus said: "You are going to hear of wars and reports of wars" (Matthew 24:6). Book 2 of the Histories is a Roman record of such a year: the East waiting while the West fought (2:6), and Tacitus's remark on how old the human craving for power is (2:38). It also names the Jewish war at its last stage, with only Jerusalem left (2:4). How much of Matthew 24 this year fulfills is read differently; see the sections on the readings.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:4; Histories of Tacitus 2:6; Histories of Tacitus 2:38; Matthew 24:6-7; Luke 21:9; Luke 21:20

sections.b: Tacitus shows Rome greeting each emperor in turn: the people cheered Vitellius at the games of Ceres (2:55), then watched the army march in (2:89) and saw soldiers camp in the unhealthy Vatican district (2:93). He ends his survey with Rome "great and wretched" (2:95). Revelation's "Babylon the Great" (Revelation 17:5) is read by many as Rome.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:55; Histories of Tacitus 2:89; Histories of Tacitus 2:93; Histories of Tacitus 2:95; Revelation 17:5

sections.b: Tacitus says the war broke out when Gessius Florus was procurator, that Cestius Gallus, governor of Syria, fought several battles with little success, and that Vespasian, sent by Nero, took the level country and all the cities except Jerusalem within two summers (5:10, in Church and Brodribb). Book 2 picks up the story in AD 69: only the siege of Jerusalem remained (2:4), and when Vespasian turned to the throne, Titus was left to press on in Judea (2:82). Josephus says Vespasian sent Titus from Alexandria with picked forces after Vitellius fell, and Titus marched by Gaza, Ascalon, Joppa and Caesarea (Jewish War 4.656-663).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:4; Histories of Tacitus 2:82; Histories of Tacitus 5:10

sections.h: What the New Testament says beforehand
sections.b: Luke records Jesus's warning: "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20), and "Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:24). He also said of the temple, "not one stone will be left on a stone" (Luke 21:6). Christians differ on how much of the Olivet Discourse this war fulfilled; see the page on the Olivet Discourse.

sections.h: Berenice in Acts and in Roman writers
sections.b: Acts spells her name Bernice: "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13). She arrived with Agrippa "in grand display" for Paul's hearing (Acts 25:23) and stood when the king stood (Acts 26:30). Tacitus says some thought Titus turned back from Rome for love of her (Histories 2:2) and that she backed Vespasian in AD 69 with her gifts (2:81). Suetonius says Titus later sent her away from Rome (Titus 7). Josephus says she was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I (whose death is told in Acts 12), sister of Drusilla, the wife of Felix (Acts 24:24), and sister of Agrippa II (Antiquities 19.9.1; 20.7.1-3). Acts does not give these family ties. Verdict: very likely the same person as the Bernice of Acts.
sections.refs: Acts 25:13; Acts 25:23; Acts 26:30; Acts 24:24; Acts 12:20-23; Histories of Tacitus 2:2; Histories of Tacitus 2:81

sections.b: Tacitus says Mucianus governed Syria and Vespasian Judea, that jealousy kept them at odds until Nero fell, and that Titus then reconciled them (2:5). The Wikipedia article says he was consul under Nero and governed Syria from 67. In Tacitus he makes a speech to Vespasian (2:76-77) and takes the oath of the Syrian army at Antioch (2:80). He then held the council at Berytus and set out with the 6th legion and detachments (2:81-83). Josephus has him urge Vespasian after the soldiers proclaimed him and report the oaths of the province (Jewish War 4.10). He entered Rome the day after Vitellius died (Wikipedia; Histories 4:11).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:5; Histories of Tacitus 2:76-83; Histories of Tacitus 4:11

sections.b: According to the Wikipedia article, he was born into a rich Jewish family of Alexandria, was procurator of Judea about AD 46-48 and prefect of Egypt from 66, and later served as chief of staff to Titus at Jerusalem. Josephus says Claudius sent Cuspius Fadus to Judea "and after him Tiberius Alexander" (Jewish War 2.11.6), and that he "did not continue in the religion of his country" (Antiquities 20.5.2). The traditional reading is that he left Judaism; the Wikipedia article says some recent scholars think Josephus meant only that he took service with Rome. Tacitus says he made the legions swear to Vespasian on 1 July (2:79). Tacitus calls him an Egyptian by birth who governed the province (1:11), and credits him with starting the movement for Vespasian (2:79). The Bible does not name him; Alexandrians appear in Acts 6:9, Acts 18:24 and Acts 27:6.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:11; Histories of Tacitus 2:74; Histories of Tacitus 2:79; Acts 6:9; Acts 18:24

sections.h: Alexandria in Acts and in AD 69
sections.b: Acts mentions the synagogue of the Alexandrians in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9), "a Jew called Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth" (Acts 18:24), and two ships "out of Alexandria" (Acts 27:6; Acts 28:11). Tacitus says the move to hand the empire to Vespasian began there, when Tiberius Alexander made the legions swear on July 1st (2:79). Josephus calls it the greatest city after Rome and says Vespasian settled affairs there before turning to Rome (Jewish War 4.656).
sections.refs: Acts 6:9; Acts 18:24; Acts 27:6; Acts 28:11; Histories of Tacitus 2:79

sections.b: Acts: "A man named Cornelius lived in Caesarea. He was a centurion in the unit called the Italian Cohort" (Acts 10:1); Paul is sent there under escort "to Felix, the governor" (Acts 23:23-24); and "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13). Tacitus says Vespasian went to Caesarea, "the capital of Judea" (2:79), and Josephus says Vespasian returned to Caesarea after finishing the places near Jerusalem (Jewish War 4.10). Titus gathered his forces there for the siege (Jewish War 4.663).
sections.refs: Acts 10:1; Acts 12:19; Acts 23:23-24; Acts 25:1; Acts 25:13; Histories of Tacitus 2:79

sections.h: Cyprus in Acts and at Paphos
sections.b: Barnabas was "a Levite born in Cyprus" (Acts 4:36). Paul and Barnabas sailed there and went "through the whole island as far as Paphos," where they met the magician Bar-Jesus and the proconsul Sergius Paulus (Acts 13:4-12). Later ships passed it on Paul's voyages (Acts 21:3; Acts 27:4). Tacitus says Titus sailed past Rhodes and Cyprus, went to Paphos to see the temple of Venus and consulted its priest Sostratus (2:2-4); Suetonius says Titus consulted the oracle of Paphian Venus about his voyage (Titus 5). The Atlas gives Paphos at 34.707, 32.574.
sections.refs: Acts 4:36; Acts 13:4-13; Acts 15:39; Acts 21:3; Acts 27:4; Histories of Tacitus 2:2-4

sections.h: The games in the Histories and the New Testament
sections.b: In Book 2, gladiators serve as troops (2:11, 2:35); the amphitheater at Placentia burns (2:21); Roman Knights are forbidden to disgrace themselves in gladiator schools and the arena (2:62); Vitellius's generals put on gladiator shows (2:67, 2:71, 2:95). Paul writes: "God has put us apostles on show last of all, like people sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world" (1 Corinthians 4:9), and "I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus" (1 Corinthians 15:32). He also pictures the racecourse (1 Corinthians 9:24-25), and Hebrews says "you were put on display like a show in the theater" (Hebrews 10:33).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 2:11; Histories of Tacitus 2:21; Histories of Tacitus 2:35; Histories of Tacitus 2:62; 1 Corinthians 4:9; 1 Corinthians 9:24-25; 1 Corinthians 15:32; Hebrews 10:33
